questions.question: How does Constellation Energy's disclosed view of nuclear fuel supply risk differ from Cameco's discussion of uranium supply risk, given their different positions in the nuclear fuel supply chain?
questions.golden_answer: Constellation Energy (a nuclear utility / fuel buyer) states in its FY2023 10-K that it 'does not anticipate difficulty' obtaining the uranium concentrates, conversion, enrichment, or fabrication services it needs, framing fuel procurement as a manageable, diversified-supplier risk. Cameco (a uranium producer/miner) instead describes deep producer-side geopolitical supply risk in its FY2025 AIF -- citing the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the 2024 Niger mine suspension, Kazakhstan supply-chain challenges, and sanctions/import-export restrictions as factors causing governments and utilities to re-examine sourcing from higher-risk jurisdictions.

agent.answer:
Constellation Energy discusses nuclear fuel supply risk from the perspective of a nuclear fleet operator and fuel buyer. It says nuclear fuel is procured through long-term contracts for uranium concentrates, conversion, enrichment, and fabrication services, including some contracts sourced from Russia, and that it manages this risk with inventory, multi-year forward contractual coverage, and a diverse set of domestic and international suppliers to protect against supply disruptions, near-term price volatility, and supplier concentration risk [8310ae7f-2a58-5c54-9107-0816f31eacc7][e2694351-8b9a-513a-8148-2d185ea6f494]. In its 2023 filing, Constellation states that it does not anticipate difficulty obtaining the uranium concentrates and related services needed for its nuclear fleet [8310ae7f-2a58-5c54-9107-0816f31eacc7]. It also frames the risk as one of fuel cost and availability, noting exposure to price fluctuations, availability restrictions, counterparty default, and geopolitical risk, and warning that non-performance by suppliers could materially adversely affect its financial statements [84bb3805-b2bf-558c-9d16-a65962129172].

Cameco discusses uranium supply risk from the perspective of an upstream uranium and fuel cycle supplier. Its filings emphasize that demand for uranium and nuclear fuel is increasing while future supply is not keeping pace, with heightened supply risk driven by geopolitical uncertainty, shrinking secondary supplies, and underinvestment in new capacity [8eaf0a61-2e0d-52d4-b8cb-d4318a89ad97][ecb536c1-3f35-52a7-8aae-8f2b0489a15a][2c425312-5d83-5871-956e-7af0e0dd1faf]. Cameco says this has pushed utilities to re-evaluate near-, mid-, and long-term fuel supply chains and has led to stronger long-term contracting and competition to secure uranium, conversion, and enrichment services from proven suppliers in geopolitically attractive jurisdictions [8eaf0a61-2e0d-52d4-b8cb-d4318a89ad97][ecb536c1-3f35-52a7-8aae-8f2b0489a15a][2c425312-5d83-5871-956e-7af0e0dd1faf]. Cameco also explicitly says that geopolitical uncertainty and years of underinvestment have shifted supply risk from producers to utilities [ce378232-9ff7-558a-ba18-701635e13c53][66b1b74f-c6b5-58dc-9221-607620ac0b0c].

So the disclosed difference is that Constellation presents supply risk mainly as a procurement and continuity risk that it believes it can manage through diversification, inventory, and long-term contracting, whereas Cameco presents supply risk as a broader market shortage and geopolitical supply problem that is increasing competition for fuel and shifting risk onto utility buyers [8310ae7f-2a58-5c54-9107-0816f31eacc7][e2694351-8b9a-513a-8148-2d185ea6f494][ce378232-9ff7-558a-ba18-701635e13c53].
